title: Jim Shepard - Blooming on the Battlefield: Relationships, Rivals, and Romance in Gameplay
speaker: Jim Shepard
summary: Jim Shepard (Dungeonmans) proposes replacing single-axis faction reputation with per-NPC relationship values that drive procedural stories during gameplay. He separates 'like' from 'respect' into a two-axis grid, applies it to foes as well as allies, and shows how each quadrant changes how NPCs answer requests and behave at critical moments, using The Princess Bride and a Paladin/Rogue party as examples. NPC personality flags interpret game events to move these values. He then adds an opt-in romance axis, defines love for gameplay, proposes a combat-partner payoff and continuation after death, and warns that guesswork is not gameplay. Q&A covers magic charm effects, communicating hidden states with emoji, and pruning noisy events.

insights.claim: Per-NPC relationship systems are fuel for procedural generation and let relationship stories happen during gameplay rather than outside it.
insights.detail: Shepard frames the talk around techniques for defining NPC relationships and their effects on the player, which he believes wholeheartedly are useful input to procgen systems.
insights.quote: The reason for this is because it is really cool fuel for your procgen systems. I believe that wholeheartedly.

insights.claim: Standard faction reputation is a single linear number that takes NPCs from not knowing you to adoring you through grinding, which is simple but silly.
insights.detail: Shepard says games keep this simple because they track dozens of factions, so tracking multiple numbers per faction seemed too much; he believes we can do better.
insights.quote: So typically these are straight lines, one exciting dimension of travel and it's simple. I do believe we can do a little bit better.

insights.claim: Like/dislike values should apply to foes as well as allies: an enemy with opposing goals can still like you, and an ally can think you are a jerk.
insights.detail: Shepard uses The Princess Bride: Westley likes Inigo Montoya and shows mercy, is indifferent to Vizzini, and loses his cool against Humperdinck's men. A foe who hates you acts irrationally and aggressively, which players can exploit.
insights.quote: Just because somebody has an opposite goal from you they can still like you. Also your allies can think you are a jerk

insights.claim: Foes can form opinions of the player during combat from fighting style, taunts, critical choices like showing mercy or rescuing hostages, and even impressive gear; outside combat, reputation precedes you.
insights.detail: Shepard lists ways a foe's like or dislike can move during and outside a fight.
insights.quote: During a conflict when you are fighting them the things you do in the fight, your style, your technique choices might impress them, might not.

insights.claim: Model NPC relationships with two independent axes, like and respect, forming a grid whose quadrants produce distinct behaviours.
insights.detail: Respect asks whether the NPC thinks you are good at your job and handle difficulty; default starting respect depends on personality. The two values move independently but interact.
insights.quote: These two values can move alongside each other but we have to remember that they are two different distinct values that are not linked.

insights.claim: In the like/respect grid, an ally who likes but does not respect you gives small help but not valuable gear, while a foe who likes and respects you may take risks to help or become a true rival.
insights.detail: Shepard's mission example: a liker-non-respecter gives gold but not a +1 assault rifle, which would end up in an enemy's inventory. A foe who likes you might drug the guards' soup so you survive. A foe who likes and respects you may switch sides or seek to prove they can beat you, making a great rivalry.
insights.quote: if you build up a true rival as a foe who likes and respects you and great conflict on the mountain top somewhere, that's boss

insights.claim: An ally who respects but dislikes you supports the mission but not you, while a foe who neither likes nor respects you underestimates you, which the player can exploit.
insights.detail: Shepard: the respecting-but-disliking ally doesn't care if you die so long as the mission succeeds. A foe holding you beneath contempt ignores you, so you can surprise them.
insights.quote: So an ally here is supporting the mission, but not you.

insights.claim: NPCs view gameplay events through personality flags to adjust like and respect, which then determine their responses to requests and behaviour during critical events.
insights.detail: Splitting treasure: the traditionalist Paladin respects you more, the selfish Rogue likes the gold but thinks you are a sucker. Overhealing the Paladin with a powerful scroll insults and angers him, but the survival-first Rogue respects it.
insights.quote: personality flags on NPCs. Respond to gameplay values to adjust like and respect values.

insights.claim: Relationship values let scripted-feeling moments emerge procedurally, such as an ally who likes but doesn't respect you tossing a potion and abandoning you, or a shopkeeper who hates but respects you selling his best gear at four times the price.
insights.detail: Shepard says events usually scripted with hardcoded NPCs can instead come from personality flags reacting to game events.
insights.quote: Usually, when you think about neat game events, there are things we may end up scripting with maybe, you know, hard coded NPCs. This stuff can be procedural.

insights.claim: Romance in a roguelike should be opt-in because it brings high stakes and some players don't want it; once they opt in, misfortunes are fair game.
insights.detail: Shepard defines love for gameplay as a desire for long-term intimacy of any type paired with a need to feel desired in return, distinct from casual hookups.
insights.quote: I believe you should require players to opt-in checkbox

insights.claim: A roguelike romance payoff can be a top-tier side-by-side combat ally of player-character strength, which also inspires your followers and adds to procedural history.
insights.detail: Shepard contrasts this with typical game romance rewards (scripted tender cutscenes or fan service). A couple's deeds can be recorded in the procedural history, not just dragon kills.
insights.quote: It's the highest tier of side by side combat ally.

insights.claim: Romantic partners can provide continuity after death: if player A dies, partner B can carry on the story.
insights.detail: Shepard acknowledges this departs from permadeath. B could keep playing and perhaps marry again, or never remarry.
insights.quote: maybe one of the pair gets killed, and the other one can pick up the pieces

insights.claim: Affection can be modelled as a single float from no attraction to maximum, built up when an NPC inclined toward you sees you act in ways that raise like or respect, including how you treat others.
insights.detail: Shepard collapses varied emotions into an average value; long-term relationships rank higher than new excitement. NPCs judge how you interact with others, like being rude to a waiter on a date.
insights.quote: if they are inclined to fall for you they might a little more every time they have an opportunity to like you or respect you

insights.claim: When players must woo NPCs, the game must make clear what they want, because guesswork is not gameplay and arbitrary failure is no fun.
insights.detail: Shepard warns against an NPC rejecting flowers because their mother died of 'floweritis', ruining the chance unfairly.
insights.quote: You have to make it clear what they are looking for. Guesswork is not gameplay and be careful when they fail.

insights.claim: Unrequited affection should have gameplay consequences, both for NPCs into the player (distracting behaviour) and for the player character falling for someone (combat debuffs, stuttering).
insights.detail: Shepard rejects the parade-of-suitors model. Players may need to cut someone from the party or match them with someone else; this is unfair like starvation or misread scrolls, and opting in means 'you asked for this'.
insights.quote: If an NPC's into you and you're not returning it they may behave differently.

insights.claim: NPC relationship states can be communicated cheaply with emoji like hearts, question marks and frowns instead of large amounts of writing.
insights.detail: In Q&A Shepard says he favours transparency because it makes player choices easier; emoji convey reactions regardless of dialect. Deceptive NPCs need clever hints, e.g. via a charisma check.
insights.quote: You could do this with emoji. Hearts pop up. Question marks. Frowns. Angry.

insights.claim: Personality-flag event lists are a possibility set to prune: drop events irrelevant to your game or that players trigger so often they skew values.
insights.detail: Asked about thousands of tiny events per adventure, Shepard says refine to the events that matter and find a way around constantly tripped ones.
insights.quote: If there's something a player does all the time that is always sending the numbers to be screwy, you don't do that

insights.claim: Magic like charm can move like, respect and affection values temporarily, swinging back the other way when it wears off.
insights.detail: Answering an audience question about charm spells and succubi, Shepard says if these values are open to the procedural engine, magic can affect them.
insights.quote: When it wears off, it swings in the other direction.
